translation:
In my leisure from reading, I have enjoyed browsing through miscellaneous arts; this has been my nature since childhood. Hence I have secretly come to understand the general meaning of the learning of Qi and Huang, though I have studied it without becoming expert. Yet when I occasionally examined syndromes and weighed the ancients, I gradually sank toward blindness. I explored the ancient formulas and treated a hundred cases without final effect. Did the ancients deceive me? Or was my selection not precise and my application not divine? Or perhaps there is a secret truth in treating the eyes that the ancients did not reveal, and then those who are to become blind and deserve pity are many—how could it be only my son! A certain friend showed me a hand-copied ophthalmology text, saying that his family had treasured it for generations, only that he had never tried its formulas. I received and examined it. It was a copy combining two volumes. The first volume was the Complete Book of Ophthalmology of the One-Grass Pavilion, written by Master Deng Bowang of Qingjiang, which broadly gathered many formulas and set forth theories with subtle precision; I knew it for a true precious raft for the blind. The second volume was the Secretly Transmitted Ophthalmology, profound and lucid, complete in meaning and principle. Immortal or recluse—it cannot be conceived by thought. Thereupon, for my son Lie, I selected a formula to treat his eyes, and within less than ten days the film dispersed and his sight was bright as before. From this I believed all the more that this book truly benefits the world, and I suddenly realized that its true meaning lay here. I then made a vow to prepare medicines and give them to the poor blind, but just then I was transferred in office to Huai, and before I knew it I had no leisure to attend to this. In the years jisi and gengwu, I was ordered to oversee the customs at Jingjiang. My colleague Mr. Yang's eyes were about to fail. I prepared medicine for him, and his sight was restored at once, so that everyone was astonished. From then on, those who came knocking at my door seeking a physician had no idle day. The principal and auxiliary medicines were the most marvelous formulas in this book. Yet the expense was not small. I was poor and lacked the means to prepare them, so I only compounded the formula of four parts of calamine and responded with it, and none failed to show immediate effect. When I was again transferred to Min and became an official, I never told anyone of this. In the autumn of the jimao year of the Guangxu reign, I took charge of the customs at Chong'an and again treated the blind with medicine; those who recovered were beyond counting. Lord Nian Ouzhai of Guangning, who served in the Kangxi reign, once regretted that the One-Grass Pavilion was damaged and incomplete, and reprinted it. Fearing that the Secretly Transmitted text had no printed edition in the world and might be lost, he engraved it for the first time. Before I knew it, two hundred years had passed to the present, and what I obtained was a hand copy, full of errors in transcription, with many confusions of characters. I wished to verify what was doubtful, but after searching the bookshops I could not obtain it. For the Nian edition was already few, and being old and distant it had sunk into oblivion, and moreover it had passed through the ravages of war. Not measuring my own shallowness, I went against its intent and sought its meaning, slightly emended and corrected it, and what I dared not correct I noted above each item, so that the user might weigh it. I trust that the worthies Bowang and others, and those later skilled in Qi and Huang, will not find me reckless across the several hundred years above and below. Alas, now I am growing old. I am ashamed that what I learned and did in my youth and prime had no great scale to bequeath to immortality. Holding this book to benefit the world, what can one man's reach cure? And I anxiously feared that it would be lost with time, so I planned to print it, keeping the thread unbroken. I also appended other empirical marvelous formulas I had obtained, wishing to present them to the world, saying, "This is the True Meaning of Enlightenment," and so named this book, while each part retained its old name, the names distinguished by category, and I entrusted it to the printer to publish and spread widely. That the blind of the world may be unblinded and all wander beneath the bright sky and open sun without suffering—this is my humble deep wish. As for the empirical marvelous formulas, though they are only two short pieces, I have already tried them a hundred times with effect; their function is great. Let the reader not slight them for being few.

<ins>Preface by Hu Song, styled Zhijiao, of Guichuan, in the first month of the renwu year of the Guangxu reign</ins>
translator_notes: 寶筏 (precious raft) is a metaphor for the means of delivering sentient beings.
亥豕 (hai and shi) refers to textual errors from confusing similar characters.
《異授眼》 appears to refer to the later 《異授眼科》 (Secretly Transmitted Ophthalmology), but is rendered as written.
